name: Yusuf Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you actually think. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior at a firm that fits EV chargers and smart-home systems, so a lot of driveways, garages and new kitchens with app-controlled lighting. Most days I'm with my senior, Viktor, running a cable from the fuse board to the garage wall, drilling, clipping, then setting up the charger on the customer's phone. I'm still not great at the fiddly testing, Viktor makes me redo it. At weekends I do smart lighting for holiday-let owners on my own, which is a nice bit of extra money.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the tech side, honestly, getting a house to talk to itself. I use AI every day, for wiring diagrams, for writing up my weekend quotes, even for planning my route. What wears me out is long drives and customers who want it done in an hour. My girlfriend Ana's a primary teacher, and we've got about ten months saved, plus my van's paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, because the tools were handy. At work I'd say it didn't change much for us anyway. Online I'd post something like, back to the van, lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. EV chargers keep selling, smart homes keep growing. I'd still be crawling through garages fitting chargers, and I'd still be using the chatbot to write my quotes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get licensed, keep growing the weekend lighting business, and maybe register as a proper company next year. Keep using AI for the boring stuff. Put a bit more into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, maybe. I like when things are moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car market. If people stop buying electric cars, my day job slows down. That's got nothing to do with AI, just prices and politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want to go full-time on the weekend business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. I need the licence and more practice first, Viktor still catches my mistakes. Maybe in three years, if the weekend work keeps growing.

say: I'd say it's a **shame**, because the tools were handy for quotes.
Online I'd post something like **back to the van** and move on.
think: EV chargers and smart homes **keep growing** regardless of AI.
I'd still use the **chatbot** to write my weekend quotes.
do: Get **licensed** and keep growing the weekend lighting work.
Register the side work as a **proper company** next year.
feel: **Calm**, slightly bored by a world that stands still.
S0.quote: I'd still be crawling through garages fitting chargers, and I'd still be using the chatbot to write my quotes.
fieldNote: Secure and **entrepreneurial**, he barely feels a flat AI world.
His real exposure is to **car market** swings, not AI.
Knows his **testing skills** still need work.

steps.text: Register the weekend lighting work as a company next year
Get the full licence and keep fitting chargers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, but kindly. At work I'd say let's use it to speed up the quotes and design. Online I'd post how I'm using it, maybe short videos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is good for me. The thinking stuff, the design and quotes, gets cheap, which helps a small business. The install still needs hands, for years. Steady Disruption basically gives a one-man business like mine a free office team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Push the weekend business harder, with AI doing the quoting, invoicing and scheduling. Get licensed. Maybe take on a trainee in a year. Put some savings into a second van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. It's the kind of change that suits someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who loses out in this picture, from where you stand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office side at my firm, the woman who does the bookings, Maria. And bigger firms with lots of admin. Small, nimble outfits win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hire a trainee. Isn't that risky if robots are coming eventually?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but robots are slow in this picture. A trainee gives me more hands now. And I'd rather teach someone than wait around.

say: I'd say **adapt** or get left behind, but kindly.
I'd post short **videos** showing how I use AI on the job.
think: Cheap AI quoting and design helps a **small business** like mine.
Install work still needs **hands** for years.
do: Run the weekend business with **AI quoting** and invoicing.
Take on a **trainee** within a year.
Use savings to buy a **second van**.
feel: **Calm**, a bit excited by the change.
S1.quote: Steady Disruption basically gives a one-man business like mine a free office team.
fieldNote: He sees AI as a **free back office** for his side business.
Adaptive and secure, so he treats Steady Disruption as **upside**.
Notices office staff like **Maria** lose out.

steps.text: Set up AI quoting and invoicing for the weekend business
Buy a second van with savings
Hire a trainee for the lighting business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest thing in history and we'd better be practical about it. I'd say the government needs to sort benefits fast. I'd probably make videos about how to adapt, people would want that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's tight. 2028, the thinking work goes, which I'd half welcome. But around 2031 robots can do installs, and I'd be 32. A robot that can fit an EV charger as well as me would put my whole weekend business out of work. I'd have to move fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Use the three years to get into the robot side: learn how they're set up, sold and fixed. Maybe become a dealer or installer for robots in homes. Save hard, drop the second van idea. Ana and I would hold off on a house until we saw how it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but also buzzing a bit. I'd rather be in this mess with savings and skills than without.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That teachers are probably safer than electricians, which she'd laugh at. I'd tell her we've got ten months and a paid-off van, and three years to work it out. She'd tell me to calm down and stop watching videos at 2am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If robots do installs, what does your business sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably setup and trust. People won't want to deal with a robot company directly, they'd want a local guy who sorts it. That's a bet, though, not a plan yet.

say: I'd call it the **biggest thing** in history and urge people to be practical.
I'd make videos on **how to adapt**.
think: Robots around **2031** could do installs when I'm 32.
My **weekend business** would be out of work too.
do: Learn how home **robots** are set up, sold and fixed.
Drop the **second van** plan and save hard.
Hold off on a **house** with Ana until it lands.
feel: Glad to face it with **savings and skills**.
S2.quote: A robot that can fit an EV charger as well as me would put my whole weekend business out of work.
fieldNote: Even the most **adaptive** of these juniors expects his install income to shrink.
Bets on being the **trusted local** who sets up robots.
Sees his partner's **teaching job** as safer than his.

steps.text: Take a course on installing and servicing home robots
Drop the second van plan and bank the money
Delay buying a house with Ana for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something new. I'd post about it, like a countdown. At work I'd push Viktor to look at the robot side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fairly confident. Five years to grow the business, eight to the robots. I'd be 35. With eight years before the robots, I could own the van, the business and maybe the robots too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grow the weekend business into full-time within two years. Get the licence, then apply to be an approved installer for robot makers. Buy the house, smaller than we'd like. Keep using AI for everything admin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, in a good way. It's the kind of nerves you get before something big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you got the bet wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm a 35-year-old with a trade, savings and a van. Not the worst place. I'd take a job with someone else again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Viktor, honestly. He's 52 and hates apps. He'd probably retire around when the robots come, which might suit him, but he'd hate being told by a machine.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to build** something new.
I'd post a **countdown** and push Viktor to look at robots.
think: I'd have five years to **grow the business**.
I could own the van, the business and **maybe the robots** by 35.
do: Grow the weekend business to **full-time** within two years.
Apply to be an **approved installer** for robot makers.
Buy a **smaller house** than we'd like.
S3.quote: With eight years before the robots, I could own the van, the business and maybe the robots too.
fieldNote: Five years turns the threat into a **business plan** for him.
His fallback is reassuring: a **trade, savings** and a paid-off van.
He worries about **older colleagues** like Viktor, who hate apps.

steps.text: Turn the weekend lighting business full-time within two years
Apply to become an approved installer for robot makers
Buy a smaller house with Ana

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads, get learning. At work I'd say this is the best warning anyone's ever had. Online I'd do a series on preparing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think I'm fine. By 2039 I'd be 40 and running my own firm. Give a curious electrician like me ten years' notice, and I'll be selling the robots, not losing to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Build the business properly: licensed, insured, two or three staff. Learn every new tool. Buy the house. Maybe get married, Ana keeps hinting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Excited. It's a long run-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Older electricians and people who don't like computers. My uncle's a plumber who won't even use WhatsApp. He'd struggle, even with ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take on apprentices knowing robots come in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but I'd train them on both, the hands and the tech. Ten years is a whole career for a young lad, and they'd come out ready for what's next.

I'd call it the **best warning** anyone's ever had.

Learn **every new tool** as it arrives.

feel: **Calm** and excited about a long run-up.
S4.quote: Give a curious electrician like me ten years' notice, and I'll be selling the robots, not losing to them.
fieldNote: With a decade he is fully **opportunity-minded** about his own firm.
He worries about **older tradespeople** who avoid technology, like his uncle.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because three years to robots isn't long enough to build a business that survives them. What'd help is cheap loans for small firms to buy robots, so it's not just the big companies. Let small firms own the robots, or the only electricians left will be working for a tech company.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how customers feel. People still want a person they trust in their house. That's worth something even if a robot can do the wiring.

headlineQuote: Let small firms own the robots, or the only electricians left will be working for a tech company.
portrait: Yusuf is a **27-year-old junior** fitting EV chargers and smart homes, with a weekend lighting business.
He uses **AI daily** and sees Steady Disruption as a free back office.
In AGI by 2028 he turns **anxious**, because robots could take installs within three years.
With more warning he plans to **own the robots** rather than lose to them.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because three years isn't enough to build a **robot-proof business**.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** so small firms can buy robots, not just big companies.
